name: CookieFlame
author: Zoobu

sections.description:
CookieFlame is a cookie consent plugin for WordPress that does three things most other free plugins do not. It finds the cookies on your site automatically by watching real visitor sessions. It runs entirely on your own server with no outside connections. And it shows the right banner for each visitor based on where they are, rather than showing a single GDPR banner to the whole world.

It is built by [Zoobu] and the full product site is at cookieflame.com.

🔍 Cookie discovery, continuously

Most consent plugins expect you to know which cookies your site sets. CookieFlame does not. A lightweight beacon watches real visitor sessions in the background and reports any cookies it has not seen before. New plugin installed? Its cookies surface automatically. Tracking tag changed? Picked up next time a visitor triggers it. No scheduled scans, no headless browsers, no external scanning service.

For a one-off inventory you can also run an on-demand Discovery scan from the admin. Browse your own site as logged in, watch the discovery bar accumulate cookies and detected services, click Finish when done.

🌍 Correct behaviour per region

CookieFlame detects visitor country and shows the banner that region actually requires:

  • EU, UK, EEA, Switzerland: full two-step GDPR opt-in banner with Accept, Manage Preferences, and Decline
  • California and other US states with similar laws: compact CCPA opt-out notice with a Do Not Sell link
  • Brazil (LGPD) and South Africa (POPIA): GDPR-style opt-in banner
  • Everywhere else: no banner, all cookies auto-granted

Detection uses three layers in order: Cloudflare and other CDN country headers first (zero latency, works with every caching setup), then a local MaxMind GeoLite2 database if uploaded, then a browser timezone heuristic as a last-resort fallback. If all three fail, the plugin defaults to GDPR opt-in for safety rather than silently granting consent.

🔒 No outside connections

CookieFlame does not load JavaScript from any content delivery network, does not call any geo API, does not phone home. Every part of the consent flow runs on your server and in the visitor’s browser. The only optional outbound request is Google Tag Manager itself, if you enter a GTM container ID in the settings (see the External services section below).

This matters because a consent tool that itself sets third-party cookies is an awkward contradiction, and because self-hosted plugins keep working during outages of services you did not choose to depend on.

🚫 Server-side script blocking

When a visitor has not granted consent, CookieFlame rewrites tracking scripts in the HTML output so the browser does not execute them. This happens before the page leaves your server, which means it works with any caching stack: WP Rocket, LiteSpeed, Cloudflare APO, W3 Total Cache, and others all hold the correct pre-modified HTML. A lighter JavaScript layer handles scripts injected later by GTM or other plugins.

Known trackers are blocked from the moment you install the plugin. Ten services ship with built-in patterns: Google Analytics, Google Ads, Google Tag Manager, Microsoft Ads, Meta and Facebook, Twitter and X, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Reddit, TikTok. Anything else you classify in the Cookie Manager gets a matching block rule generated automatically.

🪟 Iframe facades

YouTube, Vimeo, Google Maps, Spotify, SoundCloud, Dailymotion, and Elementor video widgets are replaced with click-to-accept placeholders until the visitor grants consent. The iframe source is stripped synchronously before the embed has a chance to contact its origin.

📊 Google Consent Mode v2

All seven Google consent signals are managed automatically and set to denied by default before any tag runs. When a visitor grants consent, the correct signals update immediately. Returning visitors keep their stored choices, with the signals restored before GTM loads (so the first dataLayer push is already correct).

Works with a GTM container ID you paste into the settings. No separate GTM consent template, no additional configuration. The plugin also injects the body noscript tag in the correct position.

🛡️ Global Privacy Control

GPC is detected automatically and suppresses marketing consent for CCPA visitors. Required by California, Colorado, Connecticut, Texas, and nine other US states. Turning GPC off later restores the visitor’s original stored choice rather than overwriting it.

📜 IAB TCF v2.2

A TCF v2.2 stub is registered on every page so ad-tech vendors that need TCF signals can read them.

🚀 Lightweight and framework-free

The frontend JavaScript is a single 37 KB file (12 KB gzipped) with no jQuery and no framework dependencies. A separate facades bundle is only loaded on pages that actually contain a blockable embed. The Discovery bundle only loads for administrators during an active scan.

👨‍💻 Developer-friendly

  • Event API with CustomEvents: cc:ready, cc:update, cc:accept-all, cc:decline-all, cc:save
  • Public JavaScript API for reading consent state and showing the banner on demand
  • Per-category onAccept and onReject callbacks
  • Extension points via WordPress filters and actions
  • Optional consent log endpoint for audit trails

✨ Want automatic classification?

CookieFlame Pro adds automatic cookie classification using a central database and AI. You click Auto-Identify All, and the plugin classifies every unclassified cookie with vendor, category, and purpose, then generates the blocking rules automatically. Flat annual pricing by number of sites, no pageview limits. Learn more at cookieflame.com.

📋 Compliance note

CookieFlame provides tools that help support compliance with GDPR, CCPA, LGPD, POPIA and similar regulations. Compliance itself is the site owner’s responsibility and depends on how the plugin is configured. For legal advice, consult a qualified professional.

External services

CookieFlame is a self-hosted plugin. By default it does not contact any external service from the visitor’s browser, and it does not phone home.

There is one optional external interaction, only if the site owner configures it.

Google Tag Manager (optional)

If the site owner enters a Google Tag Manager container ID on the CookieFlame Tag Managers settings tab, CookieFlame injects the standard Google Tag Manager script (https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtm.js) into the site front-end under the visitor’s consent. This script is provided by Google and is loaded from Google’s servers when the page is viewed.

  • What is sent: standard Google Tag Manager request, including the container ID and whatever browser request data Google receives for any embed.
  • When: only if the admin has set a GTM container ID, and only when a visitor loads a page and has consented.
  • Google Tag Manager terms: https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/tag-manager/use-policy/
  • Google privacy policy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

If no GTM container ID is set, no request is made.

Microsoft UET (Bing Ads tag, optional)

If the site owner enters a Microsoft UET tag ID on the CookieFlame Tag Managers settings tab, CookieFlame injects the standard Microsoft UET loader script (https://bat.bing.com/bat.js) into the site front-end. The loader is provided by Microsoft and is loaded from Microsoft’s servers when the page is viewed.

The UET runtime reads Microsoft Consent Mode v2 signals from the dataLayer that CookieFlame already manages, so the loader honours visitor consent internally: tracking events do not record until the visitor has granted Marketing consent. The loader script itself is fetched on every page load while a UET tag ID is configured.

  • What is sent: the UET tag ID, plus the standard browser request data Microsoft receives for any third-party script load (visitor IP, user agent, page URL, referer).
  • When: every page load while a UET tag ID is configured, except for visitors whose browser sends the Do Not Track header in which case CookieFlame suppresses the injection entirely.
  • Microsoft Advertising agreement: https://about.ads.microsoft.com/en/resources/policies/microsoft-advertising-agreement
  • Microsoft privacy statement: https://privacy.microsoft.com/en-gb/privacystatement

If no UET tag ID is set, no request is made.

Consent log endpoint (optional, site-owner-nominated webhook)

If the site owner enters a URL in the Consent Log endpoint setting, CookieFlame sends a JSON record of each consent decision to that URL from the visitor’s browser via navigator.sendBeacon (with a fetch fallback for browsers without sendBeacon). The default for this setting is empty, in which case nothing is sent. The destination URL is nominated by the site owner; terms and privacy obligations for that URL are the site owner’s responsibility, not CookieFlame’s.

  • What is sent: a JSON payload containing an anonymous ID, an ISO-8601 timestamp, the action that produced the record (accept-all, decline-all, save, or one of the region-based auto-grants), the per-category consent decision (necessary, preferences, analytics, marketing), the compliance mode (gdpr, ccpa, none), the visitor country code, the page URL, the user agent string, the TCF v2.2 flag, the Global Privacy Control flag, the consent policy version, and the plugin version. No cookie values are included. No IP address is included in the payload, although the receiving endpoint will of course see the visitor IP via the underlying HTTP request, the same as any other request.
  • When: every time the visitor’s consent state is set. This includes banner actions (accept-all, decline-all, save) and region-based auto-grants for visitors outside GDPR regions and for CCPA opt-out visitors.

If no Consent Log endpoint URL is set, no request is made.

Domain strings in the plugin code

The plugin code contains many third-party domain names (for example, connect.facebook.net, googletagmanager.com, and similar). These are pattern strings used for local matching only. They identify scripts that may already be present on the admin’s site so CookieFlame can detect them, show them to the admin in the Cookie Manager, and block them until the visitor has given consent. CookieFlame does not fetch from these domains.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the cookieflame folder to /wp-content/plugins/, or install via Plugins > Add New in the WordPress admin
  2. Activate the plugin through the Plugins menu
  3. Go to CookieFlame in the admin menu to review settings

That is it. The plugin works immediately with sensible defaults. The ten built-in tracking services are blocked before any visitor can trigger them, and the banner shows correctly for each region.

For best geo detection, either run Cloudflare (the plugin reads the CF-IPCountry header automatically) or upload a free MaxMind GeoLite2 database on the Geo Detection tab. Neither is required.
sections.faq:
Do I need to know which cookies my site sets?

No. CookieFlame watches real visitor sessions and reports new cookies to the Cookie Manager automatically. You classify them when you are ready, and the plugin generates the blocking rules for you.

Does this work with Google Tag Manager?

Yes. Enter your GTM container ID on the Tag Managers tab and the plugin injects both the head script and body noscript tag in the correct positions. All GTM tags that respect Google Consent Mode will see the denied state on load and wait for consent.

Does this work with Cloudflare, WP Rocket, and other caching setups?

Yes. Script blocking runs server-side in the PHP output buffer, so the cached HTML already has the correct tags rewritten. Cloudflare is specifically supported for geo detection via the CF-IPCountry header on all plans including free.

One exception: Cloudflare Rocket Loader rewrites scripts at the edge after PHP has run, which defeats the blocking layer. Rocket Loader must be disabled when using CookieFlame. The plugin detects this and shows a warning if it is active.

What happens for US visitors?

US visitors see a compact CCPA opt-out notice at the bottom of the page with a Do Not Sell My Personal Information link. Cookies are auto-granted by default because CCPA uses an opt-out model, and the visitor can revoke consent through the notice.

What happens for visitors outside the regulated regions?

No banner is shown and all cookies are auto-granted. CookieFlame does not show GDPR banners to visitors whose region does not require them.

Does the plugin contact any external service?

By default, no. Geo detection reads CDN headers first, then a local MaxMind database if you have uploaded one, then the browser timezone as a last resort. No external geo API is called. The plugin does not load scripts from any CDN and does not phone home.

The one optional external request is Google Tag Manager, but only if you have entered a GTM container ID in the settings. See the External services section for full details.

Does it handle Global Privacy Control (GPC)?

Yes. GPC is required by twelve US states and the plugin detects the browser signal automatically. For CCPA visitors with GPC active, marketing consent is suppressed before any tag runs. Turning GPC off later restores the visitor’s original choice.

Can I customise the banner text and colours?

Yes. Every string shown to visitors is editable through the Settings tab, and the banner supports both light and dark themes. For per-language versions, use WPML or Polylang with the standard WordPress translation pipeline.

What is CookieFlame Pro?

Pro adds automatic cookie classification. Instead of classifying each cookie manually, you click Auto-Identify All and the plugin uses a central database of known cookies plus AI to classify them with vendor, category, and purpose. Pro also adds tighter monitoring intervals, a more detailed digest email, and automatic MaxMind database updates. Pricing is flat annual by site count with no pageview limits. See cookieflame.com for details.

Is my visitors’ data safe?

CookieFlame does not collect visitor data. IP addresses are hashed for rate-limiting and never stored raw. Cookie values are never transmitted, only their name and a shape classification (uuid, timestamp, and similar) used for identification. The plugin stores consent decisions in a first-party cookie on the visitor’s own browser.
sections.changelog:
5.3.0

  • Cookie monitoring now ignores cookies that come with a visitor’s browser rather than from your site. Some browser extensions write the “already accepted” cookies of other consent tools (such as Complianz, CookieYes, Cookiebot, OneTrust or Didomi) onto every site they visit, and these were being reported as your site’s cookies. A consent tool’s cookie is now ignored when that tool doesn’t run on your site: its plugin isn’t active, its script isn’t on the page, and no script on the page wrote the cookie.
  • Cookies written by a browser extension’s own code are ignored too.
  • Cookies ignored this way go on the Permanently Ignored list with the reason, and the list now shows why each cookie was ignored. Restoring one keeps it monitored from then on.
  • The Cookie Manager and the Cookie Discovery count leave these cookies out too, including ones your own browser extensions add. Cookies that came with your browser during Cookie Discovery go on the Permanently Ignored list with the reason. Cookies on the Permanently Ignored list no longer show in the Cookie Manager just because they are in your own browser.
  • On update, other consent tools’ cookies that were already reported are moved to the Permanently Ignored list. Cookies you classified yourself are left alone.
  • Fixed: the “consent plugin detected” conflict warning could be set off by CookieFlame’s own list of cookie names rather than by another consent plugin on the page.
  • Cookie Manager: the last column is now “Status”. Each cookie shows one label for where it stands (Known, Auto-Identified, Classified, Added by you, Changed by you, or Not identified yet), and cookies that aren’t identified yet say where they came from: found by your scan, reported by visitors, or seen in your own browser.
  • Cookie Manager: Remove and Ignore permanently are now one “Remove…” link that asks why. “My site doesn’t use it any more” takes the cookie off your list, and it comes back if it’s seen again. “It’s not from my site” puts it on the Permanently Ignored list for good.
  • Cookie Manager: with CookieFlame Pro, the padlock is now a “Lock as correct” button. A locked cookie keeps its vendor, category and purpose, even when you re-identify.
  • Cookie Manager: the small help buttons beside each link are gone. Each link explains itself when you hover over it, and the Status column’s help button explains every label and action.
  • Improved: when another consent tool’s code is on your pages, the warning now says so in plain words (“Cookiebot found on your pages”), names the page and the text to look for, and lists where such code usually lives (plugins, page builder custom code such as Elementor > Custom Code, the theme’s header, or a header and footer scripts plugin). It used to say a plugin was installed even when the code came from somewhere else.

5.2.0

  • Cookie monitoring now records which script first wrote each new cookie: a third-party script’s domain, or the WordPress plugin or theme that set it. Previously only the full list of third-party scripts on the page was known. Cookie values are never read or sent.
  • Cookie monitoring now checks again later in the visit, a few seconds after the visitor changes their consent choice, and when they leave the page, so cookies set after consent or after the first few seconds are found.
  • Fixed: when a page reported several new cookies at the same moment, some could be lost, because the reports overwrote each other when saving. Reports are now saved one at a time, so every new cookie is kept.
  • The cookieflame_new_cookie_discovered action now fires after the cookie’s details are saved and passes them as a fourth argument (pre-existing flag, value type, writer). Listeners using three arguments are unaffected.
  • Tested up to WordPress 7.1.

5.1.1

  • Cookie declaration shortcode tag is now [cookieflame_declaration] (previously [cookieconsent_declaration]). If you embed the cookie declaration on your Privacy Policy page, update the shortcode tag.
  • URL fields on the Settings page (Privacy URL, CCPA URL, Consent log endpoint) now use esc_url_raw, the WordPress URL sanitiser, in place of sanitize_text_field.

5.1.0

  • Cookie Monitoring tab redesigned for clarity. The page now leads with the two controls that matter (Monitoring on/off and Update interval) and trims the long-form intro and guidance copy that buried them.
  • New: the Update interval dropdown shows CookieFlame Pro intervals (15 minutes, 1 hour, 4 hours) inline as disabled options labelled “(Pro)”, so you can see at a glance what an upgrade adds without leaving the page. They unlock when CookieFlame Pro is active.
  • Removed the Monthly interval. It was producing digests so far apart that newly discovered cookies were already weeks stale by the time the email arrived. Existing sites set to Monthly will move to Daily on update.
  • Removed the in-page “Clear monitoring history” button. The 30-day auto-purge handles staleness without intervention; for the rare support case where a full reset is needed, the new WP-CLI command “wp cookieflame purge-beacon-seen” replaces the button.
  • Filter contract change for developers extending the interval list: cookieflame_interval_buckets now passes tier-aware entries (each entry shaped [‘minutes’ => N, ‘tier’ => ‘free’|’pro’]). Plain integers from third-party filter contributors are still accepted and default to the free tier for back-compatibility.

5.0.2

  • Fixed: Geo Detection now correctly recognises the Cloudflare CF-IPCountry header again. Sites fronted by Cloudflare without a MaxMind database installed were falling through to the GDPR opt-in safety default for every visitor, which meant CCPA-eligible US visitors saw the GDPR banner instead of the CCPA notice, and visitors in regions where no banner is required also saw the GDPR banner. The Geo Detection admin panel was reporting “Not configured” on Cloudflare-fronted sites for the same reason. No setting changes are required; geo detection resumes automatically on update.

5.0.1

  • Hardened consent boot: the five wp_head injection hooks (consent defaults, config, frontend script, Google Tag Manager, Microsoft UET) now register at deep-negative priorities so other plugins cannot hook ahead of CookieFlame and push tags before consent signals are set.
  • Beacon endpoint refactored: the per-IP rate limit now runs as a REST permission_callback, rejecting bursts at the routing layer above the request handler. The same check still runs inside the handler as a belt-and-braces guard.
  • Defensive shutdown handler added for the output buffer: walks the buffer stack at end of request and flushes only CookieFlame’s own buffer if it remains open, leaving any caching or optimisation plugin buffers above it untouched.
  • Database queries against the beacon-seen table reworked to inline the WordPress table prefix directly in each SQL literal, with rationale comments on the remaining advisory warnings.
  • wp_unslash applied consistently to display-only query parameters on the Cookie Monitoring tab.
  • Readme: added an Upgrade Notice section.

5.0.0

  • Initial public release.
